title.p: At the edge of the map

epigraph.p: A page is another way of making room.

section.p: The harbour woke before the town. A line of pale light rested on the water, and the boats turned slowly at their moorings. Mara carried a notebook with no itinerary in it. On the first page she had written a single question: what will we notice if we stop hurrying?

At the end of the quay, a small bell marked the hour. Nobody seemed to obey it. A gull inspected the empty baskets, a mechanic warmed his hands around a cup, and the crew checked each knot twice. There was comfort in work whose purpose could be seen.

The navigator unfolded a chart that had been repaired along its creases. Its narrow channels looked certain on paper. From the deck, the coast was all overlapping shapes. She explained that a map is useful because it leaves things out, and dangerous for exactly the same reason.

By noon the town had become a bright square behind us. The engine settled into a patient rhythm. We passed the notebook around the table and added one observation each: the taste of salt on an apple, the green underside of a wave, the silence after a rope stopped moving.

There was no grand discovery that afternoon. We made tea, watched the changing shore and found a sheltered place to wait for the tide. In the log, these became three short lines. In memory, they took up the whole day. A page can hold both kinds of distance.

Near evening, clouds opened above the western ridge. The light reached the water before it reached the boat. Everyone looked up at once, then returned to ordinary tasks. Mara left a little space beneath her last sentence. Some things, she decided, should have room around them.
